frontmatter.title: Workhorse
frontmatter.subtitle: Software Engineer – Automation & Operations. PHP, MySQL, AWS and AI-assisted helpdesk automation.
frontmatter.author: Chris Garlick

blocks.title: What they're hiring for
blocks.intro: A broad, practical engineering role on a PHP / MySQL / AWS platform: ship Jira tickets with AI-assisted tools, keep the helpdesk moving with automation, and keep the platform healthy.

items.label: Title
items.value: Software Engineer – Automation & Operations

items.label: Stack
items.value: PHP, MySQL, AWS

items.label: Day to day
items.value: Jira tickets, scoped, built, reviewed, tested and deployed with their existing AI-assisted workflow

items.label: The big project
items.value: Their AI-powered RAG pipeline for the helpdesk: better ticket enrichment, then automated drafting, resolution and escalation

items.label: Also
items.value: SQL and migrations, CI/CD, AWS monitoring and alerting, implementation support, the outsourced infrastructure team

items.label: Level
items.value: Mid-level. Strong SQL, sound fundamentals, deployment, automation and cloud experience

items.label: Note
items.value: PHP is *beneficial but not essential*, so your PHP is a clear advantage

blocks.title: Read between the lines
blocks.body: **Improving existing systems rather than always building from scratch** and **confident in assessing the quality and reliability of AI-generated outputs** are the two phrases to land. They already have the AI tools; they want someone who makes them *reliable*, not someone who just generates more code.

blocks.title: What they want, what to show
blocks.intro: Every responsibility in the job description, with the evidence to bring. Fill the gaps tonight.

rows: How you take a vague ticket to a scoped, tested, deployed change.
How you use Claude Code day to day, and how you review what it writes.
An LLM or retrieval feature you built; how you'd measure and improve it.
A query you optimised, a schema you designed, a migration you ran safely.
A pipeline you built; a repetitive task you automated away.
Metrics and alarms you've set up, and an incident you caught or diagnosed.
A production bug you tracked down: how you found it, how you fixed it.
Helping non-developers (helpdesk, implementation) and outside specialists.

blocks.title: Your strongest stories
blocks.body: **Typeset**: a render API you built and run in production, which hit memory limits on a small server; you diagnosed the OOMs, added swap, and know concurrency and timeouts are next. That is *monitoring, investigation and operations* in one story. **Claude Code**: you build with coding agents every day and review their output. **PHP / Laravel**: years of it.

blocks.title: From Jira ticket to production
blocks.intro: They want ownership: you help scope the ticket, not just pick it up.

blocks.title: Why it matters
blocks.body: **Take ownership of Jira development tickets, help scope technical requirements and deliver** is the first responsibility listed. Show a repeatable process.

items.title: Understand the problem
items.detail: Who reported it, what they expected, how to reproduce it. Ask before you build.

items.title: Find the code
items.detail: Trace the path through the codebase; note what else touches it.

items.title: Write acceptance criteria
items.detail: What done looks like, edge cases, and what's out of scope. Add it to the ticket.

items.title: Plan with the agent
items.detail: Give the AI tool the ticket, the relevant files and the constraints; agree a plan first.

items.title: Small, focused changes
items.detail: One concern per PR; no drive-by refactors in a bug fix.

items.title: Test
items.detail: A failing test that reproduces the bug, then the fix. Cover the edge cases from scoping.

items.title: Review
items.detail: Read every line yourself before anyone else does, then a peer review.

items.title: Deploy
items.detail: Through the pipeline, with a way to roll back; database changes go first and stay backward compatible.

items.title: Close the loop
items.detail: Check it in production, update the ticket, tell the person who reported it.

blocks.title: Say this
blocks.body: *"I treat the ticket as the start of a conversation. I'll reproduce it, write down what done looks like, then build it in small reviewed steps, and I don't close it until I've seen it working in production."*

blocks.title: Reviewing code you didn't write
blocks.intro: They already use AI tools. The skill they're hiring for is judging the output.

blocks.title: Why it matters
blocks.body: **Reviewing generated code to ensure changes are well-targeted, maintainable, secure and properly tested.** Those four words are their checklist; use them back.

rows: Does the diff only touch what the ticket needs? Agents love to "improve" nearby code. Revert anything unrelated.
Does it match the codebase's patterns and naming? No new abstractions for one use, no duplicated helpers that already exist.
Parameterised SQL, escaped output, authorisation checks on every route, no secrets in code or logs, input validated.
Tests that would fail without the change. Watch for tests that only test mocks, or assertions weakened to pass.

items: **Confident invention**: a function, column or config option that doesn't exist. Check it does.
**Silent scope creep**: a 40-line fix becomes a 400-line diff.
**Happy path only**: nulls, empty lists, timezones and concurrency get missed.
**Swallowed errors**: `try/catch` that hides the real failure.
**Tests bent to fit**: the test changed to match buggy behaviour, not the other way round.
Project instructions (e.g. `CLAUDE.md`) with conventions, commands and "don't touch" areas.
Make the agent run the tests and linters before it says it's done.
Reusable prompts or skills for common tickets: a bug fix, a migration, a new endpoint.
Automated review on every PR as a first pass, never a replacement for a human.

blocks.title: Say this
blocks.body: *"I use Claude Code every day, and the more I use it the more I see my job as setting it up well and reviewing hard. I read every diff as if a new colleague wrote it."*

blocks.title: How a RAG pipeline works
blocks.intro: Retrieval-augmented generation: find the relevant information first, then let the model answer from it.

blocks.title: Why it matters
blocks.body: Maintaining and developing **their existing AI-powered RAG pipeline** is the most distinctive part of the job. Expect detailed questions here.

items.title: Collect sources
items.detail: Help articles, past resolved tickets, product docs, release notes, known issues.

items.title: Chunk
items.detail: Split into passages of a few hundred tokens, by heading or section, with a little overlap.

items.title: Embed and store
items.detail: Turn each chunk into a vector; store it with metadata (product, version, date, source URL).

items.title: Build the query
items.detail: From the ticket's subject and body, plus customer context: plan, product, version.

items.title: Retrieve
items.detail: Top matches by vector similarity, ideally combined with keyword search (hybrid), filtered by metadata.

items.title: Rerank
items.detail: Reorder the candidates with a reranker so the best few go to the model.

items.title: Generate
items.detail: The model drafts an answer *only* from the retrieved context, with citations.

rows: Better chunking, hybrid search for error codes and product names, metadata filters, reranking.
Re-index on change; store dates; prefer newer sources; retire old articles.
Answer only from context, require citations, allow "I don't know", lower temperature.
An evaluation set of real past tickets with known good answers; measure every change.

blocks.title: Drafting, resolution and escalation
blocks.intro: The job description says *progressively*. Automate in stages, with a human in the loop until the numbers say otherwise.

items.title: Add context to every ticket
items.detail: Customer's account, recent errors from logs, related articles and similar past tickets, for the agent to see.

items.title: Classify
items.detail: Category, product area, urgency and sentiment, so tickets reach the right person.

items.title: Suggest a reply
items.detail: The helpdesk agent edits and sends. Nothing goes to the customer unreviewed.

items.title: Measure
items.detail: How often drafts are sent unchanged, lightly edited or discarded. That's your quality signal.

items.title: Auto-send for narrow, safe categories
items.detail: Password resets, how-to questions with a clear article, only above a confidence threshold.

items.title: Always offer a human
items.detail: Every automated reply says how to reach a person.

items.title: Clear rules
items.detail: Low confidence, angry customer, billing or data issues, security, repeated contact, or a likely bug go to a person.

items.title: Hand over with context
items.detail: The escalation carries the summary, what was tried and the retrieved sources.

blocks.title: Risks to raise before they do
blocks.body: **Prompt injection**: ticket text is untrusted input; it must never be able to change the model's instructions or trigger actions. **Personal data**: what goes to the model provider, and is it logged? **Wrong answers at scale**: one bad article can now reach hundreds of customers, so monitor and keep a kill switch.

blocks.title: Say this
blocks.body: *"I'd start by measuring what the pipeline does today against real past tickets, because you can't improve retrieval you can't measure. Then automate the narrow, safe cases first and widen it as the draft-acceptance rate proves it."*

blocks.title: SQL you should be fluent in
blocks.intro: Strong SQL is the first thing in the candidate profile. Expect a live query or a whiteboard question.

blocks.title: Why it matters
blocks.body: **Write and maintain SQL, manage database updates, schema changes and migrations, and ensure database integrity and performance.** Fluency here is non-negotiable.

rows: INNER vs LEFT; LEFT JOIN … WHERE b.id IS NULL to find missing rows.
GROUP BY with HAVING to filter groups; COUNT(DISTINCT …).
ROW_NUMBER, RANK, LAG, running totals; MySQL 8 has them.
WITH … AS for readable multi-step queries; recursive CTEs for trees.
Composite indexes follow the leftmost-prefix rule; cover the WHERE then the ORDER BY.
Look for type = ALL (full scan), "Using filesort", "Using temporary", rows examined.
InnoDB; BEGIN / COMMIT; default isolation REPEATABLE READ; keep them short.
Foreign keys, NOT NULL, unique constraints, correct types (DECIMAL for money).

blocks.content:
-- Latest ticket per customer, with how many they've raised
WITH ranked AS (
    SELECT t.*,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY created_at DESC) AS rn,
           COUNT(*)     OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id)                          AS total
    FROM tickets t
    WHERE created_at >= NOW() - INTERVAL 30 DAY
)
SELECT customer_id, id AS latest_ticket, subject, total
FROM ranked
WHERE rn = 1 AND total >= 3
ORDER BY total DESC;

blocks.title: Performance and safe schema changes
blocks.intro: How to find a slow query, and how to change a big table without taking the site down.

items.title: Find it
items.detail: Slow query log, Performance Insights on RDS, or performance_schema.

items.title: Read the plan
items.detail: EXPLAIN, or EXPLAIN ANALYZE (MySQL 8.0.18+) for actual timings.

items.title: Fix the cause
items.detail: Add or reorder an index, avoid functions on indexed columns, fix N+1 queries in the app, paginate.

blocks.content:
EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT id, subject FROM tickets
WHERE status = 'open' AND assigned_to = 42
ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20;

-- Serves the filter and the sort in one index
CREATE INDEX idx_tickets_status_assignee_created
    ON tickets (status, assigned_to, created_at);

-- Not this: a function on the column can't use the index
-- WHERE DATE(created_at) = '2026-10-23'
-- Do this instead
-- WHERE created_at >= '2026-10-23' AND created_at < '2026-10-24'

items.label: Expand, then contract
items.value: Add the new column, deploy code that writes both, backfill in batches, switch reads, then drop the old column in a later release.

items.label: Online DDL
items.value: MySQL 8 can add many columns with ALGORITHM=INSTANT, and many index changes with INPLACE, without locking writes.

items.label: Big tables
items.value: pt-online-schema-change or gh-ost copy the table in the background and swap it in.

items.label: Backfills
items.value: In batches of a few thousand rows, with a pause between, so you don't flood replication.

items.label: Always
items.value: A backup or snapshot first, tested on a copy of production data, and a rollback plan.

blocks.title: CI/CD and reliable releases
blocks.intro: Maintain and improve their pipelines, and automate the repetitive work.

blocks.title: Why it matters
blocks.body: **Maintain and improve existing CI/CD pipelines, automate repetitive development tasks and support reliable software releases.** Note *existing*: understand it before you change it.

items.title: On every push
items.detail: Install dependencies (cached), lint and static analysis (PHPStan), run the tests.

items.title: On merge
items.detail: Build one artefact, deploy it to staging, run smoke tests.

items.title: To production
items.detail: The same artefact, with migrations first, then a health check and an easy rollback.

blocks.content:
# GitHub Actions: the shape of a PHP pipeline
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    services:
      mysql: { image: mysql:8.0, env: { MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD: root, MYSQL_DATABASE: test } }
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: shivammathur/setup-php@v2
        with: { php-version: '8.3' }
      - run: composer install --no-interaction --prefer-dist
      - run: vendor/bin/phpstan analyse
      - run: vendor/bin/phpunit

rows: Less to go wrong; easier to find what did.
Old and new code both work during the deploy.
Ship code dark, turn it on for some customers first.
Automatic rollback on failed health check
Bad deploys fix themselves in minutes.

blocks.title: Automating repetitive tasks
blocks.body: Good examples to offer: generating release notes from merged PRs, setting up a local environment with one command, refreshing a staging database with anonymised data, and AI review of every PR as a first pass.

blocks.title: AWS monitoring and alerting
blocks.intro: Availability, memory, CPU and performance are named explicitly. Know which need extra setup.

blocks.title: Why it matters
blocks.body: **Implement and maintain AWS monitoring and alerting, covering system availability, memory utilisation, CPU capacity, performance and potential issues.** This is a gap they want filled.

blocks.title: The detail that shows you've done it
blocks.body: EC2 sends **CPU** to CloudWatch by default, but **not memory or disk space**. Those need the **CloudWatch agent** installed on the instance. RDS reports memory as **FreeableMemory** without it.

rows: ALB HealthyHostCount; a Synthetics canary or uptime check
Any host unhealthy, or the check fails twice
Near max connections, or lag growing

items.label: Route alerts
items.value: CloudWatch alarm → SNS topic → email, Slack or PagerDuty.

items.label: Avoid noise
items.value: Alert on symptoms customers feel; use evaluation periods so a spike doesn't page anyone; composite alarms to combine signals.

items.label: Dashboards
items.value: One CloudWatch dashboard per service: traffic, errors, latency, saturation.

items.label: Logs
items.value: Ship app and PHP error logs to CloudWatch Logs; metric filters turn error lines into alarms.

blocks.title: Typeset: memory on a small server
blocks.intro: Your own production system, and exactly the kind of issue they want caught early. Rehearse it.

items.label: Situation
items.value: Typeset, a PDF render API you built and run in production on a server with 960 MB of RAM.

items.label: Problem
items.value: Large renders ran out of memory and the process was killed (OOM).

items.label: What you did
items.value: Diagnosed it as memory, not a code bug; added swap as an immediate fix so renders complete.

items.label: What's next
items.value: Limit how many renders run at once and add a timeout, so one big job can't starve the rest.

items.label: The lesson
items.value: Monitor memory, not just CPU, and alert before it runs out, not after. That's the point of the role's monitoring work.

blocks.title: Make it theirs
blocks.body: Close with how you'd apply it at Workhorse: *"On AWS I'd install the CloudWatch agent so memory is visible, alarm at 85%, and look for which requests drive the peaks."*

items.title: Scope it
items.detail: Who's affected, since when, what changed? Check recent deploys first.

items.title: Gather evidence
items.detail: Logs, metrics and the database, around the time it started. Reproduce it if you can.

items.title: Mitigate, then fix
items.detail: Roll back or work around to stop the harm; then find and fix the root cause.

items.title: Write it up
items.detail: What happened, why, and what stops it happening again. Add the alarm that would have caught it.

blocks.title: Working with the outsourced infrastructure team
blocks.body: Escalate with evidence: the time it started, the metrics, the logs, what you've ruled out. It saves them hours and earns trust. Learn from each handover so next time you can fix it yourself.

blocks.title: PHP refresher
blocks.intro: PHP is a bonus for them, which makes it an advantage for you. Be ready to talk about legacy code too.

rows: Typed properties, constructor promotion, enums, match, readonly, named arguments, nullsafe ?->.
Prepared statements with bound parameters, always. Never build SQL from strings.
Dependencies and PSR-4 autoloading; commit composer.lock.
PHPUnit or Pest; PHPStan for static analysis.
Add tests around it before changing it; refactor in small steps; don't rewrite.

blocks.content:
<?php declare(strict_types=1);

final class TicketRepository
{
    public function __construct(private readonly PDO $db) {}

    /** @return list<array{id: int, subject: string}> */
    public function openFor(int $agentId, int $limit = 20): array
    {
        $stmt = $this->db->prepare(
            'SELECT id, subject FROM tickets
             WHERE status = :status AND assigned_to = :agent
             ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT :limit'
        );
        $stmt->bindValue(':status', 'open');
        $stmt->bindValue(':agent', $agentId, PDO::PARAM_INT);
        $stmt->bindValue(':limit', $limit, PDO::PARAM_INT);
        $stmt->execute();

        return $stmt->fetchAll(PDO::FETCH_ASSOC);
    }
}

blocks.title: Say this
blocks.body: *"I've worked a lot in PHP and Laravel, so I can be useful in the codebase from the first week, and I'm comfortable in older code: I'd put tests around something before I change it."*

blocks.title: Stories to have ready
blocks.intro: Use situation, task, action, result. Two minutes each, with a number in the result where you can.

rows: Something you built and run in production
Typeset: a render API in production; how you deploy, monitor and fix it.
The Typeset OOMs: memory not code, swap now, concurrency and timeouts next.
Claude Code daily: planning first, small diffs, reading every line, tests before done.
A time AI got it wrong
Have one specific example: what it invented or broke, and how you caught it.
Improving a system you didn't build
A legacy PHP or Laravel app you modernised without a rewrite.
The query, what EXPLAIN showed, the index, before and after timings.
A script, pipeline or agent workflow that saved you or a team time.
Explaining an issue to a client or support person in plain words.

blocks.title: Tonight
blocks.body: Fill in the two you're least sure of, especially *a time AI got it wrong* and *a slow query you fixed*, with real details. Specifics are what make a story believable.

items: Walk me through how you'd pick up a Jira ticket you don't fully understand.
How do you review code an AI tool has written? What do you look for?
Explain how a RAG pipeline works. How would you improve one that gives poor answers?
How would you decide when it's safe to send an AI reply to a customer without a person checking it?
What is prompt injection, and how would you protect a helpdesk pipeline from it?
Write a query: customers who raised more than three tickets in the last 30 days.
A page is slow and you suspect the database. What do you do?
How do you add a column to a table with 50 million rows without downtime?
What would you monitor on AWS for a PHP app, and how would you alert on it?
The site is down. Talk me through your first ten minutes.
Why this role, and why now?
Tell me about something you built that you're proud of.
How do you balance working independently with keeping the team informed?
What excites you about AI, and what worries you about it?

blocks.title: Questions to ask them
blocks.intro: Pick three or four that fit the conversation. They signal that you've thought about the job.

items: What does the RAG pipeline do today, and where does it fall short?
What does it index, and how do you know if its answers are good?
How many tickets a month, and which kinds would you most like automated?
Which AI development tools do you use, and what's your review process for their output?
What does the path from ticket to production look like? How often do you deploy?
Where is the codebase hardest to work in?
What monitoring is in place on AWS now, and what has gone wrong that it didn't catch?
How is the work split with the outsourced infrastructure team?
What would success look like in the first three and six months?

blocks.title: Closing line
blocks.body: *"This role covers everything I enjoy: shipping real changes, making AI tools reliable rather than just using them, and keeping a production system healthy. I'm used to owning things end to end, and I'd like to help make the helpdesk automation something the team really trusts."*
